title: Mixtures, Solutions and Separation
scope_note: Class IX concepts, with experimental inference enrichment as indicated
introduction: Understanding a mixture means more than naming a separation technique. This chapter moves from substance identity and dispersed phases through concentration and solubility to experimental designs that recover components. It teaches the property difference that makes each separation possible.

subtopics.title: Elements, compounds and mixtures
subtopics.entry_question: Salt water is transparent, and so is pure water. Are they chemically the same kind of matter?
core1a_paragraphs: An element consists of one chemical element; a compound contains chemically joined elements in a characteristic composition; a mixture combines substances without a fixed chemical combination ratio. Appearance alone cannot tell us which category we have.

A pure sample of sodium chloride is a compound represented by NaCl. Salt water is a mixture of water and dissolved NaCl, with variable concentration. Changing the amount of salt alters the mixture's composition without changing the chemical formula of either component.

Separation method is evidence: a physical process such as evaporation can recover salt from a salt solution. Decomposing the chemical compound NaCl into sodium and chlorine is a different type of transformation and cannot be achieved by ordinary evaporation.
subtopics.representation: Compare particle diagrams: pure element A; pure compound AB with all units identical; mixture of independent A and B species. Do not draw dissolved salt as undissociated NaCl molecules by default; aqueous Na⁺ and Cl⁻ are present.

worked_example.problem: Classify copper metal, pure water and salt water.
steps: Copper consists of atoms of one element: element.
Pure H₂O has characteristic combination of hydrogen and oxygen: compound.
Salt water has variable proportions of at least two substances: mixture.
worked_example.check: Try adjusting salt concentration: mixture changes continuously, but H₂O stays H₂O.

misconception.wrong: Anything transparent and uniform must be a pure compound.
misconception.why: A homogeneous mixture can look identical to a pure liquid.
misconception.repair: Use composition variability and separability, not only visual uniformity.

demands.title: Composition versus chemical identity
demands.core1a_explanation: Composition is fixed for a pure compound but variable for mixtures; connect that distinction to recoverability of components.
demands.worked_reasoning: Adding 5 g salt to 100 g water and adding 20 g salt to 100 g water can produce different mixtures, not new formulas for NaCl.
demands.independent_check: Distinguish component formula from mixture proportions.

demands.worked_reasoning: A transparent sample yields a solid residue after water evaporates; this supports a nonvolatile solute in a mixture, not a new pure water compound.

subtopics.title: Homogeneous and heterogeneous systems
subtopics.entry_question: If no particles are visible in a milk sample, does that make it homogeneous at every scale?
core1a_paragraphs: A homogeneous mixture appears compositionally uniform at the relevant observation scale; a heterogeneous mixture has distinguishable regions or phases. 'Homogeneous' is not a claim that all particles are literally identical.

Salt completely dissolved in water forms an apparently uniform solution. Muddy water has suspended particles that can vary between sampled regions. Milk may appear uniform to the eye while containing dispersed droplets at smaller scales, making scale important.
Mixing and settling can change whether an initially dispersed sample remains uniform. A classification should declare the observation scale, sampling method and time after preparation.
subtopics.representation: Show three magnification levels: visible glass, microscopic suspended droplets, molecular-scale dissolved ions. Label the scale, not only the apparent colour.

worked_example.problem: Compare salt solution and sand stirred into water after leaving both to rest.
steps: Salt remains dispersed as solvated components at ordinary concentrations.
Sand remains as separate solid grains and typically settles.
Salt water is homogeneous at ordinary observation scale; sand water is heterogeneous.
worked_example.check: Inspect different positions and wait for settling.

misconception.wrong: A mixture that looks uniform for one second is a permanently homogeneous solution.
misconception.why: Fine suspensions can appear uniform briefly.
misconception.repair: Repeat sampling over time and at an appropriate scale.

core1b.repair: Combine scattering, stability and separation evidence.

core1b.model_response: No. These observations are compatible with a colloid of particles smaller than ordinary filter-paper pores. Scattering opposes the simple true-solution classification; additional particle-size evidence may help.

subtopics.title: Solutions, suspensions and colloids
subtopics.entry_question: Why can a transparent salt solution and a cloudy colloid both resist ordinary settling?
core1a_paragraphs: A true solution has solute present at molecular or ionic scale. In a suspension, larger particles remain distinct from the medium and can settle. A colloid contains dispersed particles intermediate in behaviour; many remain stable for long periods but scatter light.

The Tyndall effect arises from scattering of light by particles or droplets in an appropriate size range. It is one clue, not a universal on/off detector without specifying concentration, wavelength and experimental geometry.

Filtration with ordinary filter paper separates many suspensions but generally does not remove truly dissolved solutes. Some colloids also pass ordinary filters; their separation can require different methods.
subtopics.representation: Compare (a) transparent salt solution with ions, (b) stable colloid with droplets causing a visible beam and (c) suspension with larger grains and settling.

worked_example.problem: A liquid scatters a narrow beam of light and remains uniform for hours. Which classification is plausible?
steps: Light scattering indicates dispersed structures capable of redirecting light.
Long-term stability weighs against a coarse rapidly settling suspension.
The evidence supports a colloidal dispersion.
A single observation does not identify the particles' chemical nature.
worked_example.result: Colloid is plausible; composition not uniquely identified.
worked_example.check: Compare ordinary filtration and microscopic size evidence.

misconception.wrong: A visible beam in any liquid proves a chemical reaction is occurring.
misconception.why: Light scattering is a physical optical effect of dispersed particles.
misconception.repair: Separate optical observations from species-changing reactions.

demands.core1a_explanation: Connect light interacting with dispersed particles to a visible beam.
demands.worked_reasoning: A colloid may show a visible beam because dispersed droplets scatter incoming light toward the observer.

subtopics.title: Concentration: mass/mass, mass/volume, volume/volume
subtopics.entry_question: Two drinks both contain 10 g sugar, but one is a cup and the other a litre. Which is more concentrated?
core1a_paragraphs: Concentration expresses an amount of solute relative to a specified quantity of mixture or solution. The denominator is essential: mass fraction uses total solution mass, whereas mass/volume concentration uses solution volume.
Ten grams sugar in 100 g solution is 10% by mass. Ten grams in 100 mL solution is 10 g per 100 mL, often written 10% m/V. These measures are not interchangeable without density information.

Dilution adds solvent while preserving the amount of nonreacting solute in the ideal model. Concentration decreases because the denominator rises; pouring away part of a well-mixed solution changes solute amount and total volume proportionally but leaves concentration unchanged.
subtopics.representation: Use a ratio bar with numerator solute mass and denominator total solution mass or volume. Explicitly label % m/m or % m/V and do not substitute solvent mass.

worked_example.problem: A 120 g solution contains 18 g solute. Calculate mass percentage.
steps: Use mass fraction = solute mass / total solution mass.
Substitute 18 g / 120 g = 0.15.
Multiply by 100 to obtain percent.
worked_example.check: 18 g solute + 102 g solvent = 120 g solution.

misconception.wrong: Use only solvent mass in the denominator for mass percentage.
misconception.why: The defined mass percentage uses total solution mass.
misconception.repair: Write the concentration definition and units before substituting.

demands.title: Track concentration under dilution
demands.core1a_explanation: Adding solvent changes total solution amount but not the mass of retained nonreacting solute.
demands.worked_reasoning: 20 g solute in 200 g solution is 10% m/m; adding 200 g water makes 400 g total at 5% m/m.
demands.independent_check: Check the numerator conserved before removing any solution.

subtopics.title: Solubility versus temperature
subtopics.entry_question: Why does heating water usually dissolve more sugar, but a dissolved gas may escape more readily?
core1a_paragraphs: Solubility is the maximum amount of a solute that can dissolve in a given amount of solvent at stated conditions and at equilibrium. The dissolved amount in an unsaturated sample can be smaller than its solubility.

For many solids in water, solubility increases with temperature; this is not universal. Gas solubility often decreases as temperature increases at fixed gas partial pressure. The actual direction depends on the substance and conditions.

Crystallisation can result when a hot saturated solution cools. An experimental calculation must specify whether solvent mass is conserved and whether the excess solute crystallises completely at equilibrium.
subtopics.representation: Draw solubility-versus-temperature curves for a hypothetical solid and gas as illustrative trends, explicitly mark hypothetical and avoid implying every substance follows the same slope.

worked_example.problem: At one temperature, salt solubility is 36 g per 100 g water. How much can dissolve in 250 g water?
steps: Ratio is 36/100 grams solute per gram water.
Multiply by 250 g solvent.
Maximum solute mass = 90 g under same conditions.
worked_example.result: 90 g of that salt can dissolve in 250 g water at the stated temperature.
worked_example.check: 90/250 = 36/100; no mistaken use of solution mass.

misconception.wrong: Solubility always rises when temperature rises.
misconception.why: Different solids and gases may show different temperature dependences.
misconception.repair: Read the specific solute curve and state fixed conditions.

demands.title: Solubility mass-balance
demands.core1a_explanation: A solubility table gives g solute per 100 g solvent, not per 100 g final solution.
demands.worked_reasoning: If maximum dissolvable salt is 40 g per 100 g water, 150 g water can dissolve 60 g at equilibrium.
demands.independent_check: Check total solute conserved.

subtopics.title: Separation: crystallisation, distillation and chromatography
subtopics.entry_question: How can pure water be recovered from salty water without chemically destroying salt?
core1a_paragraphs: Separation depends on differences in physical properties: volatility, solubility, adsorption, particle size and phase behaviour. A successful method targets the relevant difference rather than a familiar equipment name.

Crystallisation can recover dissolved solid while leaving some impurities in solution. Simple distillation heats a solution, collects vapour and condenses it in a separate receiver; nonvolatile salt generally remains behind. Fractional distillation is useful when volatile components have relatively close boiling ranges.

Chromatography separates components that distribute differently between a mobile phase and a stationary phase. Spots appearing at different positions provide evidence of distinct movement, not automatically of chemical purity or unique identity.
subtopics.representation: Diagram a distillation train: heated salt water, vapour path, condenser, receiver, salt residue; arrows follow the path of water only, never salt 'evaporating' with water in the simple model.

worked_example.problem: Choose a method to recover both salt and water from sea-water-like brine.
steps: Identify water as volatile and salt as largely nonvolatile.
Use simple distillation to condense water vapour into a receiving vessel.
Recover salt from concentrated residue by further evaporation/crystallisation.
Check contamination and recovery losses independently.
worked_example.check: Mass ledger for collected water, salt and residue plus apparatus losses.

misconception.wrong: Filtration separates dissolved salt from water.
misconception.why: Ordinary filter pores are vastly larger than dissolved ions and solvent molecules.
misconception.repair: Choose a technique based on dissolved state and property contrasts.

demands.core1a_explanation: The apparatus separates substances by vapour formation and condensation, not by filtering tiny ions.
demands.worked_reasoning: Brine heated to boil produces vapour enriched in water; condenser returns it to liquid separate from nonvolatile salt.
demands.independent_check: Track where each component goes.

subtopics.title: Separation: centrifugation, sublimation and coagulation
subtopics.entry_question: If ordinary filtering fails to remove tiny suspended particles, what other physical distinction can we exploit?
core1a_paragraphs: Centrifugation accelerates sedimentation of dispersed components that differ in density and size under suitable conditions. It changes separation rate, not chemical identity. A centrifuge does not separate every molecule merely by spinning.

Sublimation occurs when a solid enters the gas phase without passing through an ordinary bulk liquid phase under specified conditions; substances such as iodine may be separated from non-subliming mixtures in some classroom demonstrations.

Coagulation deliberately destabilises certain colloids, causing small dispersed particles to aggregate into larger structures that may settle or filter. The process must be chemically appropriate to the dispersion and its conditions.
subtopics.representation: Provide three sketches with arrows: spin tubes with sediment, subliming solid to cold surface, colloidal small clusters to larger flocs. Each figure labels which property differences are exploited.

worked_example.problem: An ink-like colloidal suspension passes ordinary filter paper. Name a possible next method and why it may help.
steps: Identify that the dispersed particles are too small for ordinary filtration.
Consider coagulation if the colloid can be destabilised safely, forming larger aggregates.
Filter or settle the resulting aggregates.
Check whether the treatment changes the chemical analyte of interest.
worked_example.result: Coagulation followed by settling/filtration is one candidate route.
worked_example.check: A separation strategy must preserve what is meant to be recovered.

misconception.wrong: All suspensions and colloids can be separated by the same filter paper.
misconception.why: Particle size and dispersion stability vary widely.
misconception.repair: State the separation mechanism and its material/size limitations.

core1b.model_response: The strong effective acceleration increases the tendency of density-different particles to move relative to liquid, often speeding sedimentation. Dissolved molecules are not automatically pelleted.

core1b.boundary: Would simply dissolving both in water have the same selective effect?
core1b.model_response: Under controlled conditions iodine can sublime to vapour and deposit on a cool surface while sand remains. Ventilation and safety controls are needed.

core1b.model_response: The initial particles pass the filter. Coagulation first produces larger aggregates that the subsequent filter can retain. The order matters, and the treatment must be chosen for the actual colloid.
